summary.text: The main sequence is the continuous, distinctive band that stars form on plots of stellar color versus brightness.
Stars spend the majority of their lives there, mainly burning hydrogen in their cores, and the Sun is one of them.
A star's place on the band is set mainly by its mass, and the more massive a star is, the shorter its time there.

items.prompt: A huge star and a small star begin burning hydrogen in their cores at the same moment. Which one leaves the main sequence first?

options.label: The small star, since it has less fuel
The huge star, since it is more massive
Both leave at the same moment
Neither leaves; all stars stay on it forever

items.explain: The more massive a star is, the shorter its lifespan on the main sequence.

items.prompt: Gravity keeps trying to squeeze a main-sequence star inward. What holds it up?

options.label: A shell of cold gas pressing in from outside
The star spinning too fast to collapse
The pull of nearby stars
A pressure gradient from the heat of core fusion

items.explain: Thermal energy from fusion radiates out from the hot core, creating a strong pressure gradient that counters collapse and keeps the star in hydrostatic equilibrium.

Mostly the difference in their names

One group was a different colour from the other

items.explain: Those stars were either much brighter than the Sun or much fainter, so he called them giants and dwarfs.

paragraphs.heading: A band on the chart
paragraphs.text: When stars are plotted by colour against brightness, they form one continuous, distinctive band. That band is the main sequence. Such colour-magnitude charts are named Hertzsprung–Russell diagrams, honouring the astronomers Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell. Stars spend most of their lives on this band, a stage when burning hydrogen in the core is their main activity. Main-sequence stars, sometimes also called dwarf stars, include the Sun, and no kind of true star in the universe is more numerous.

paragraphs.heading: What holds a star steady
paragraphs.text: When a cloud of gas collapses under gravity far enough, the heat and pressure at its core set off nuclear fusion, turning hydrogen into helium. Heat from this flows outward from the hot, dense core and sets up a strong pressure gradient. That gradient pushes back against gravity, keeping the star in a balance called hydrostatic equilibrium instead of collapsing. Where a star sits on the band depends mostly on its mass, and also on its age and chemical make-up.

paragraphs.heading: Two ways to burn hydrogen
paragraphs.text: The band is split into an upper and a lower part, according to how stars make their energy. The Sun and stars below about 1.5 M_(☉), meaning 1.5 times the Sun's mass, join hydrogen into helium in a series of steps called the proton–proton chain. Heavier stars, in the upper main sequence, mainly use the CNO cycle, in which carbon, nitrogen and oxygen act as go-betweens in turning hydrogen into helium. The proton–proton chain still runs in these stars, but it yields less energy than the CNO cycle.

paragraphs.heading: Moving the energy out
paragraphs.text: Radiation is not the only way energy travels through a star; convection also carries it. Stars where the CNO cycle dominates have convecting cores, which stir up the new helium and keep the right share of fuel in place for fusion. Lighter stars have cores where energy moves only by radiation, with convective zones near the surface. The lower the mass, the bigger the share of the star taken up by a convective envelope, and below 0.4 M_(☉) the whole star convects. Where the core does not convect, a helium-rich core builds up inside an outer layer of hydrogen.

paragraphs.heading: Metals and lifetimes
paragraphs.text: Astronomers describe a star's chemical make-up by its metallicity: the share of elements heavier than helium. By mass the Sun is now 74.9% hydrogen and 23.8% helium, leaving a metallicity of 1.3%. Higher metallicity makes a star more opaque, so energy stays packed in the core, and this hotter core speeds up fusion and shortens the star's time on the main sequence. Mass works the same way: the more massive the star, the shorter its main-sequence life. Once the hydrogen in its core is used up, a star leaves the band and becomes a supergiant, a red giant, or goes straight to a white dwarf.

paragraphs.heading: Finding the pattern
paragraphs.text: In the early 20th century, more became known about the types and distances of stars. At Harvard, Annie Jump Cannon and Edward Charles Pickering sorted stars by features in their spectra, in what became the Harvard Classification Scheme, published in 1901. In 1906 Ejnar Hertzsprung noticed that the reddest stars, types K and M, split into two groups: much brighter than the Sun or much fainter. He called them giants and dwarfs. Turning to star clusters, whose stars sit at roughly the same distance, he published the first plots of colour against luminosity and named the clear band in them the Main Sequence.

paragraphs.heading: Russell's side of the story
paragraphs.text: At Princeton, Henry Norris Russell was working along similar lines. He plotted stars' spectral types against their absolute magnitude, which is their real brightness once distance is corrected for, using stars with reliable parallaxes. He found that dwarf stars followed a clear relationship, so a dwarf's real brightness could be predicted fairly accurately. Giants, being much brighter than dwarfs, did not fit that relationship.
